Appalachian Spring. A one-act ballet choreographed by Martha Graham in 1944 to celebrate American pioneer life in the Appalachian region. The work premiered at the 1944 Coolidge Festival and captures the hope, joy, and resilience of early settlers through Graham's modernist movement vocabulary combined with folk material, making it one of the most purely American ballets and a cornerstone of American modern dance.

Aaron Copland composed the score, which incorporates the Shaker hymn Simple Gifts and employs cowboy songs and other Americana. The music won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize for Music. Martha Graham choreographed and performed the Bride role, using her revolutionary modern dance technique to express both Classical grace and raw emotional authenticity.

The narrative centers on a young bride and groom and their community: a Revivalist Preacher and his congregation, a Pioneer Woman, and attendant settlers, all celebrating a wedding and communal life in the frontier. The famous Simple Gifts variations feature soloists and ensemble performing transformations of the hymn tune, with increasingly complex geometric patterns and rhythmic variations.

Graham's movement vocabulary blends modern dance contractions, floor work, and angular shapes with Classical ballet vocabulary, creating a distinctly American modern aesthetic. The Bride's solo is a moment of tender introspection and vulnerability, capturing the emotional complexity beneath the community celebration.

The ballet premiered at the Coolidge Festival in Washington, D.C., on 30 October 1944 and has since become a repertory staple of American ballet and modern dance companies. The work connects Graham herself, the choreographer-dancer whose modernist movement vocabulary revolutionized dance, with Copland, whose populist, Americana-rich score defined American modernism. It draws on American folk culture as source material and stands as a cornerstone of modern dance.
